at.deep: Why pull won over push, and what a micro-batch actually is

items.item: Every pipeline has four positions: a source, a buffer, a sink and a cursor; which side owns the buffer depends on whether the data is pulled or pushed.
In a pull, the consumer owns the schedule and the source holds the buffer, which costs the source retention for however long the consumer takes to ask.
In a push, the source owns the schedule and the consumer must own a buffer that absorbs bursts, or it drops data.
Batch, micro-batch and streaming are the same underlying idea (a poll) at three different interval sizes, not three unrelated mechanisms.

at.deep: Why pull won over push, and what a micro-batch actually is

items.item: Shrinking the poll interval buys lower average delay and smaller burst size per delivery, measured directly: average delay and rows handled per tick both shrink together as the interval shrinks.
Batch's own largest risk is a late or silently skipped run going unnoticed, because nothing about batch itself surfaces that it didn't run.

items.item: Micro-batch's own largest risk is many small, separately checkpointed runs accumulating many small outputs (files, commits) downstream.

items.item: Streaming's own largest risk is an unbounded backlog, because nothing about a continuous feed shields the consumer from a producer's own surge the way a schedule does.
